newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: LITHUANIA-INVESTMENT FUNDS MAY INJECT LIFE INTO BOURSE.
newsitem.headline: LITHUANIA-INVESTMENT FUNDS MAY INJECT LIFE INTO BOURSE.

text.p: Lithuania's stock market, which badly needs a boost since a January bullrun fizzled out, may get the injection of life it needs with three new planned local investment funds, brokers and analysts said on Wednesday.

The top three brokerages, Vilniaus Bank, Vilfima and Suprema have all said they are planning to launch investment funds, possibly in the autumn, for the first time in Lithuania. Mendes Prior Europe is also considering a fund.
Brokers said the new funds would encourage money to come to the market by attracting peoples' savings and the disposable income of an emerging middle-class.

"We can find money from abroad but we have to boost our savings because people have a lot of money at home in their mattresses," said Margarita Starkevichiute, financial analyst at the central securities depository.
"They can invest it, but it's expensive to set up a portfolio for each citizen," Starkevichiute said. "It's cheaper to pool it in a fund."
The bourse has been in the doldrums recently and its capitalisation fell last week to 5.418 billion litas from 5.6 billion litas the week before.
But market capitalisation is still up from the end of 1996, when it was 3.6 billion litas.

The head of Suprema brokerage, Aidas Galubickas, said it was difficult to say but that its fund would probably include up to 30 official list and group A companies and have a size of around one million dollars initially.
Leading brokerage Vilfima said it would probably focus its fund on government securities.
"Our approach would be to start an open-ended T-bill fund," said Vidas Jelinskas, head of Vilfima.
"We have some experience with Treasury bills because we have a product that is very similar to an open-ended mutual fund," Jelinskas said. He declined to say how big the fund would be.
Broker Mendes Prior Europe is also considering launching a fund this year.

"The cap for the fund might be about five million litas," said Kestutis Kupshys, a broker with Mendes. Kupshys said it would probably include all of the group A shares as well as LISCO, Sema, Kalnapilis and Lithuanian Energy.
"The main problem in Lithuania is that we don't have institutional investors as players on the market," said Kazimieras Liepis, head of Mendes Prior Europe.

"Individual investors are very passive now, and there are problems in laws on insurance companies, which are prohibited from investing in equity, they can only invest in government securities," said Liepis.
The investment community has also had high hopes that the privatisation of large enterprises will also inject liquidity into the struggling bourse.

Privatisation officials at the European Affairs Ministry, which is overseeing the privatisation of 13 major enterprises by open international tender, have said they are considering selling partial stakes on the open market.
But it is still unclear when privatisation will begin to ripple onto Lithuania's stock exchange.
Observers say the bourse is ailing now in part because the falling prices since the bull run earlier this year have scared off foreign investors.
"We're waiting very eagerly for foreign investors but now the major buyers have stopped being active and nothing is happening on the market," said Vilfima's Jelinskas.
"Only after we have our own strong local investors will the market be attractive to foreigners," Jelinskas added.
According to Starkevichiute and others, the problem is not a lack of local money for investments but a matter of coaxing it to the market.

"Gambling on the capital market is quite risky," Jelinskas said. "From our experience, there is sort of a middle class in Lithuania -- doctors, architects, clerks -- and they need somewhere to put their money."
